doc.title: Nick Mondello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 19, 2022

title: Musical family and first trumpet lessons on Long Island
summary: Music filled the house; an uncle studied with Doc Cheatham, Nick got a trumpet, studied with Felix Sangenito and played Italian weddings and political events as a kid.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Great question, and I did think about that. I’ll be honest with you I thought about that before this interview. I’ve been truly, truly blessed to come from a family, not so much of musicians although there were some, two of the paternal great, great, great whatever back in Italy were bandmasters. And when I was a youngster at about five years old one of my uncles was a student of Doc Cheatham. He was a semi-pro trumpet player. But here’s the thing. There was always pervasive music in the household, predominantly from the women singing. So you grow up hearing all of these Sophie Tucker tunes and Fanny Brice tunes and tunes from the 20s and whatever. And my father, he knew Al Jolson. That’s how far back he went, okay? So in his case it was always all of the Al Jolson tunes. “Avalon,” “Sonny Boy” as a matter of fact “Sonny Boy” was one of the first tunes I remember as an infant. So there was always this music, musical environment, all the time. So it was almost a logical progression that music would take hold in some capacity, whatever it was. So having an uncle that played the trumpet, somehow I got a trumpet. I don’t recollect how. It certainly wasn’t like Clark Terry with the hosaphone but I started lessons with an old-time trumpet teacher named Felix Sangenito who has taught a number of very, very fine players including — I’m trying to remember his name, it’ll come to me in a second — but he’s taught a lot of guys, especially here on Long Island. So it was very much a progression. It was almost like no one forced you into this, but it was osmosis, okay? You know? You know I tell people the DNA is five lines and four spaces. And it was always like that. So you always were involved in the school band and what-have-you. And again, shortly after that things started to open up outside the family. They used to take me around as a little kid playing at things like weddings, you know, let’s bring the little kid up and have him play, you know, “Come Back to Sorrento” or something like that you know. Like what Frankie Avalon did in some of his video clips. Right? So you’d be playing these Italian weddings as like, “Bring the kid up,” you know let him do his thing. But of course there were no smart phones or video cameras back then. So you did that kind of thing. And then I remember taking me around to like political get-togethers for — this guy’s running for mayor, let’s have this kid come and play whatever. So he got a couple of Italian votes. You know and then like I say, things started to move outside of the family but it was reinforced by the family.
So let me ask you a question, and first of all I’m going to ask you can you move back just a little bit? Yeah. Perfect.
So we’ll just snip this out.
